title: The boy and the teacher
hookLine: tradition says young Nanak asked his village teacher what the letters really pointed to
last: BEBE NANAKI — SOMEONE SAW YOU FIRST.

lines: A QUESTION THAT STOPPED THE LESSON.
cards: Why is the sky blue? Why do we have to go to bed? Why?
A small child asks it, and then asks again, and again, until the grown-up runs out of answers and says because I said so. Somewhere along the way, right answers start to crowd that question out.

The story goes that when Nanak was about seven, his father took him to the village teacher to learn his letters, so that one day he could keep accounts like his dad. The teacher wrote out the alphabet on a wooden board.
And the boy asked a question that stopped the lesson.

teach.b: In the janamsakhis, the village teacher, a pandha, writes the letters on a wooden writing board, a patti, and tells the boy to copy them. Nanak does.

teach.h: BUT WHAT DO THE LETTERS MEAN?
teach.b: And then he asks: but what do they mean? Not what sound does this letter make. What does it point to?

The teacher, used to children who just copied, doesn't know what to say. And the boy, the story goes, begins to explain: each letter can point you toward God. The first letter, toward the one who made everything.
The next, toward truth. And so on, all through the alphabet, until the teacher bows to the student. Here's what makes it more than a legend.

teach.h: PATTI — AN ALPHABET POEM IN SCRIPTURE.
teach.b: In the Guru Granth Sahib there really is a poem by Guru Nanak called Patti, the writing board. It's an acrostic: it runs through the alphabet, and each letter opens a line about God and the soul.
In paraphrase, one letter begins a line about the one who created the world and is master of all. Another warns the mind that it will have to give an account of itself.
Some readers think Nanak composed it as a grown man, and the janamsakhi set it back in his childhood, at the moment it seemed to belong. Either way, the question is his.
Tradition also says he later learned Persian from a Muslim teacher and studied Sanskrit texts too, so he wasn't against learning. He just wouldn't stop at the surface of it.
The same boy who asked what the sacred thread was for, back on day six, asked what the alphabet was for. It's the question under his whole life.

how: Sikh children often hear this story when they begin learning Gurmukhi, and Guru Nanak's Patti, an acrostic on the alphabet in the Guru Granth Sahib, is sung in kirtan.

games.q: you're seven. the teacher has written the alphabet on a board and told you to copy it. what do you do?
o: copy it neatly and go home.
copy it, then ask what the letters really mean.
games.why: he copied it, and asked what it pointed to. the story says the teacher ended up bowing to the student.

practice: Pick one word you use every day without thinking: home, friend, sorry, work, love. Ask Nanak's question of it: what does this really point to?
Don't rush for an answer; let the word open slowly, like the letters on the teacher's board.
